title: An Information-Theoretic Perspective on Spectral Reconstruction in Lattice QCD
summary: Assessing the reliability of spectral reconstruction from finite, noisy lattice correlators requires understanding the constraints supplied by the data relative to prior assumptions. We develop an information-theoretic framework using Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergences to quantify the information supplied by the data through changes from prior to posterior probability distributions. Our analysis accounts for both changes in the probability distributions of spectral strength at individual energies and constraints encoded in correlations across the spectrum. We smear these information measures over neighboring energies using Gaussian weights to obtain a smoothed assessment at a specified energy scale. We demonstrate this framework using a hierarchical Bayesian reconstruction method with posterior sampling, applied to mock correlator data generated from a three-peak spectrum and a near-physical lattice proton correlator. These calculations show that the information measures help explain the properties of reconstructed spectra. They also provide a semiquantitative criterion for assessing how strongly reconstructed spectral structures are constrained by the data and how reliable they are in light of prior effects.

title: Constrained field-space estimators for background-field lattice QCD observables
comment: 19 pages, 3 figures, 12 tables. Code and derived data: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23869797
summary: Background-field lattice calculations extract weak-field response coefficients from correlators computed at several field strengths. We treat this extraction as linear estimation in field space and compare fixed cancellation stencils with covariance-optimized, generalized-least-squares estimators of the same coefficient, using archival nucleon double ratios on about 1000 quenched configurations at six quark masses and decuplet correlators for which exact answers follow from the lattice contractions. The fixed $O(B^4)$-$O(B^8)$ stencils are nearly coincident and cost almost nothing in precision. Weight-free null-space tests reject the two-term response model in most nucleon ensembles; whether they reject the three-term model depends on the temporal fits and on the noise of the estimated temporal covariance, which raises the null-contrast error by a factor of 1.7-2.4. With that noise included, covariance optimization gains 1-2% in precision at the five lighter masses (3-30% with two-state time fits, which also lower moments by 3-10%) and nothing on independent data halves, while its weights carry three to four orders of magnitude more leverage on omitted response modes than the fixed stencils and move the moments by up to 1.8 marginal standard errors. The decuplet controls show what such leverage does under misspecification: the first-order responses obey $μ_{Δ^+}/μ_{Δ^{++}}=1/2$ and $μ_{Δ^0}=0$ exactly. The lowest-order estimate misses the first by 10-25 standard errors. The fixed $O(B^4)$-$O(B^8)$ stencils satisfy it within errors in the production windows, whereas the correlated linear fit in $B^2$, with the same constraints as the $O(B^4)$ stencil, misses it by 3-17%; the null-space test rejects that fit's model. The results distinguish statistical precision from robustness to omitted response modes; they are not physical-point magnetic moments.

title: Flavor decomposition of the nucleon axial and tensor charges from lattice QCD
summary: We determine the nucleon axial and tensor charges using four ensembles of twisted-mass clover-improved fermions with approximately equal physical volumes of about 5.5~fm and four lattice spacings, $ a=0.05$~fm, 0.06~fm, 0.07~fm, and 0.08~fm. The mass of the degenerate up and down, strange and charm quarks are tuned to approximately their physical values. We compute both connected and disconnected contributions to determine the isovector and isoscalar charges and their flavour decomposition. For the nucleon isovector axial charge we find $g_A^{u-d}=1.263(34)(26)$, in agreement with the experimental value. For the isoscalar axial charge we find $g_A^{u+d}=0.458(16)(1)$, while for the corresponding tensor charges we find $g_T^{u-d}=0.951(21)(5)$ and $g_T^{u+d}=0.556(16)(5)$.

title: Evaluating generative samplers for lattice field theory by scale
summary: Generative samplers for lattice field theory are commonly evaluated by their effective sample size (ESS). We show that a small global ESS need not imply inaccurate long-distance observables: errors spread over many short-distance modes can dominate this diagnostic. We introduce a scale-resolved diagnostic based on the overlap between coarse-grained model and target distributions. At the lattice cutoff, this overlap determines the asymptotic ESS fraction; lower cutoffs isolate long-wavelength errors. In the exactly solvable free theory, two samplers with comparable ESS yield a $32\%$ bias and no bias in the susceptibility, respectively. In two-dimensional $φ^4$ theory near criticality, trained diffusion samplers show the same separation of scales: their path-weight ESS fraction falls rapidly over the volumes studied, while low moments of the magnetization remain close to their target values. Varying the reference parameters substantially changes infrared observables, with little effect on the log-weight variance. Given the target magnetization distribution, a marginal Metropolis test maintains an acceptance rate of order one in our tests. Combined with exact local updates, it reduces the remaining mismatch, although residual bias remains at finite relaxation length. In the free field, uniformly bounded relative errors in the proposal mode variances give a volume-independent bound on the number of updates needed for a prescribed accuracy of the chain's stationary mode variances at fixed correlation length. The target marginal must be supplied or computed separately; estimating it from the samplers' own weights can inherit the poor global overlap.

title: Markov-Shielded Typicality for Thermal Quantum States
summary: Pure states of quantum many-body systems at thermal equilibrium are known to be typical, in a sense that a randomly chosen pure state from an appropriate energy shell reproduces the Gibbs-state expectation values of most observables acting on a small subsystem. However, such typical states are intrinsically stochastic, conventionally generated from the random high-temperature state, suffer from statistical fluctuations, and do not provide a continuous connection to the ground state. Here, we introduce a deterministic variational framework for constructing a Markov-Shielded Typical (MST) state, a unique thermal pure-state representative whose local reduced density matrices closely approximate those of the Gibbs state, from the ground state up to infinite-temperature limit. Our approach reformulates free-energy minimization by replacing the nonlocal von Neumann entropy with a local, computationally tractable Markov entropy, where we establish rigorous upper and lower bounds of MST free energy to lie in the very vicinity of the thermal free energy. This framework extends the concept of typicality to deterministic pure-state representations of thermal equilibrium, offering a scalable wave-function approach with potential applications to both classical and quantum computing.

title: Exceptional Topological Bound States in the Continuum
summary: Topological phases, exceptional points, and bound states in the continuum (BICs) are three key concepts in condensed matter and classical wave physics. Their pairwise combinations have yielded a rich variety of intriguing singular modes, but the triple merger--exceptional topological BICs (ET-BICs)--has yet to be explored. In this Letter, we theoretically propose and experimentally demonstrate a universal approach for constructing such elusive exceptional structures. The system consists of four coupled topological chains: y-mirror stacking generates pairs of topological BICs, while z-stacking with biased loss yields a generalized mirror symmetry under which each pair--separated in different subspaces until their collapse--merges into an ET-BIC at a critical loss. Experimentally, using an acoustic platform with electrically tunable loss, we not only directly observe the coalescence of eigenenergies but also the coalescence of eigenstates, offering a complete verification of the ET-BIC formation. The triply synergistic ET-BICs may pave the way for wave devices that simultaneously demand robustness, sensitivity, and BIC confinement.

title: Roadmap on Nanoscale Superconductivity for Quantum Technologies
summary: In 2025, the Year of Quantum Science and Technology, we celebrate a century of quantum mechanics, witnessing a surge in activities that illuminate its inherent strangeness and drive technological innovation. Superconductivity, discovered 114 years ago, stands as a prime example, offering direct and compelling evidence of macroscopic quantum phenomena. Beyond its ability to conduct immense currents without loss, superconductivity reveals the quantum realm operating on a scale we can directly observe and manipulate. The macroscopic quantum coherence, where an ensemble of particles is described by a single wave function, leads to remarkable consequences: dissipation-less current and flux quantization - the basic properties exploited in superconducting quantum circuit fabrication. This Roadmap has been inspired by intensive discussions and collaborations emerging from the European COST Action CA21144 (SuperQuMap - Superconducting Nanodevices and Quantum Materials for Coherent Manipulation). The roadmap outlines the network's concrete activities, driving advancements in superconductor-based quantum technologies and charting future directions. Spanning fundamental research to practical applications, the roadmap incorporates insights from industry partners developing quantum computation. It begins by exploring quantum materials, highlighting how topology and electronic correlations could catalyze a quantum leap in technology. We then delve into manipulating the superconducting phase, leveraging advancements in magnetism, 3D fabrication, and tunable correlations. Further, we showcase the advanced microscopy techniques - such as angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy and scanning probes - used to visualize quantum behavior. Finally, and crucially, we detail the quantum devices developed within the network, and their transformative impact on modern quantum computing approaches.

title: On the Seven-particle Clusters of Lennard-Jones and Thomson
summary: In this Letter, we develop a graph-geometric framework and prove that the pentagonal bipyramid (PBP) is the unique global minimiser of both the seven-particle Lennard-Jones energy in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and the seven-charge Thomson energy on $S^2$, up to rigid symmetries and particle relabelling. For the Thomson problem, this strengthens a recent deterministic global-optimality certificate to numerical tolerance into an exact global-optimality and uniqueness theorem. A weak-interaction graph, defined by thresholding pair geometry, organises configuration space without imposing symmetry or discarding any pair interaction. For Lennard-Jones, pair-energy counting, graph classification, subset bounds, and force balance reduce all possible minimisers to 29 bounded domains; exact geometric certificates exclude 28, localise the survivor near the PBP, and a uniform restoring-energy estimate proves uniqueness. The Thomson proof follows the same progression: graph reduction, geometric localisation, and rigidity, but finalises through whole-domain coercivity and a global localisation theorem. The same fivefold order therefore emerges in two very different physical settings: an unconstrained cluster with a preferred bond length and purely repelling charges confined to a sphere, showing a common geometric organising principle for seven particles that is not tied to either interaction.

title: Interpretable machine learning of formation energies and band gaps in hybrid perovskites through SHAP analysis and SISSO modelling
summary: Accurate and interpretable property prediction is essential for exploring hybrid organic-inorganic perovskites. Here, we combine machine-learning screening with SHAP analysis and SISSO descriptor discovery. Using 4,456 compounds, optimized XGBoost models achieved test-set $R^2$ values of 0.99 for formation energy and 0.93 for band gap and were applied to over 180,000 candidates. Comparison across approximately 17,000 common compounds revealed broadly overlapping distributions from XGBoost and CGCNN but substantially lower predictions from UPET, suggesting potential limitations in its transferability to hybrid organic-inorganic perovskites. SHAP analysis and correlation-based pruning retained eight primary features for each property, from which SISSO derived expressions comprising four nonlinear descriptors. These expressions couple molecular and inorganic properties for formation energy and emphasize relative atomic sizes and B-site characteristics for band gap. This framework supports efficient candidate prioritization and interpretable analysis of learned structures-property relationships in hybrid perovskites.

title: Superconductivity in the Metallic Wigner Crystals of Rhombohedral Graphene: Possible Realization of an Electronic Supersolid
summary: Recent experiments on rhombohedral multilayer graphene have reported metallic Wigner crystals (MWCs), in which spontaneously broken translational symmetry coexists with mobile charge carriers. Their proximity to time-reversal-symmetry-breaking superconductivity raises the intriguing possibility that collective excitations of the electron crystal mediate pairing among the residual itinerant carriers, giving rise to a superconducting Wigner crystal---an electronic analog of a supersolid. Here we investigate this possibility using a realistic model of electron-doped rhombohedral multilayer graphene with spin and valley polarization, whose low symmetry removes the usual Cooper instability. We use self-consistent and time-dependent Hartree-Fock theory to map the evolution of the self-doping fraction and characterize the collective-mode spectrum of the MWCs, followed by a multiband linearized Eliashberg analysis of pairing. Upon increasing density, we find an instability of the MWC, triggered by a weakly dispersing unoccupied band approaching the chemical potential. Pairing remains weak deep in the stable MWC. However, on approaching the instability, we identify a collective mode composed of interband electron-hole excitations that softens. We show that this mode drives pairing at experimentally relevant temperatures. The leading pairing instability is at finite momentum and combines Fermi surface states with states in the incipient band, making a Fermi surface or single-band pairing analysis inadequate. Our results establish collective-mode-mediated superconductivity in MWCs as a viable scenario for rhombohedral graphene and motivate experimental searches for coexisting electronic charge order in its superconducting phases.

title: Renormalized symmetry probes for emergent symmetries and non-chiral lattice fermions
comment: 69 pages, 4 figures, 16 tables. Supplemental Material provided as the ancillary file supplemental_tables.pdf
summary: The degeneracy of hadron correlators in symmetry-related channels signals symmetry restoration in high-temperature QCD. RG-invariant probes of this degeneracy need care when the regularization breaks chiral symmetry, or when the symmetry is not exact in the massless action, as for the emergent chiral-spin symmetry $SU(2)_{CS}$. We renormalize the thermal and screening meson correlators of every flavor sector by the thermal correlator of the same channel in the $\bar ud$ sector at a common reference point. The symmetry ratio $κ_{AB}$ then depends on the renormalization only through the ratio $R_{AB}$. For exact symmetries, $R_{AB}=1$ and $κ_{AB}$ is RG invariant and scheme independent in mass-independent schemes. For emergent symmetries, $R_{AB}\neq1$ carries the relative logarithmic cutoff dependence of the two channels, which cancels in $κ_{AB}$, and the residual dependence on the reference scale is physical. The framework applies to Wilson, twisted-mass and staggered fermions, where $R_{AB}$ absorbs the channel-dependent renormalization, and the tensor pair $(T_k,X_k)$ keeps $R_{T_kX_k}=1$ on isotropic Wilson-type lattices. Lattice artifacts are a small correction to the chiral-spin probes $κ_{CS}$ and $κ_{fade}$, but as large as the signal of the exact-symmetry probes. For free quarks, we derive $κ_{fade}=2/3$ for every mass and separation, and $κ_{CS}\le1/3$. We apply the renormalized probes to $N_f=2+1+1$ QCD with optimal domain-wall quarks at the physical point, with $a=0.064$ fm and $T=192$-$1539$ MeV. The hierarchical restoration of the chiral symmetries from the light to the charm sectors is confirmed, and is invariant under renormalization. The $\bar uc$ and $\bar sc$ sectors have the widest chiral-spin windows, also at a tighter threshold. Thus spin-1 mesons with one charm quark are the most attractive channels for the chiral-spin regime.

title: Dynamic Scaling and Aging in Hydrodynamic Coarsening of Vapor Bubbles in a Lennard-Jones Fluid
summary: We investigate the coarsening and aging dynamics of vapor bubbles during liquid-vapor phase separation in a three-dimensional single-component Lennard-Jones fluid using large-scale molecular dynamics simulations. Following a temperature quench from a homogeneous high-temperature state into the two-phase coexistence region, vapor bubbles nucleate and grow in the liquid background. The characteristic bubble size follows a power-law growth, $\ell(t)\sim t^α$, with a growth exponent $α\simeq 2/3$, characteristic of inertial hydrodynamic coarsening. We also investigate the two-time autocorrelation function $C_{ag}(t,t_w)$ which follows waiting-time dependent relaxation, revealing aging. Furthermore, data at different waiting times collapse onto a scaling function when plotted as a function of the length ratio $\ell(t)/\ell(t_w)$, demonstrating dynamical scaling during aging. The corresponding scaling function exhibits an algebraic decay with an exponent $λ\simeq 3$. Interestingly, bubble and droplet growth exhibit distinctly different domain-growth and aging exponents despite both being disconnected morphologies.

title: Optimizing one-dimensional lithographically defined nanowires in semiconducting heterostructures
summary: One-dimensional nanowires can host remarkable electronic properties and are central to studying quantum transport. Although heterostructure-defined confinement combined with gate-defined potentials can greatly reduce the effects of impurities as measured via electron mobilities, the realization and interpretation of novel effects at this scale are complicated by disorder. Experiments on lithographically defined one-dimensional nanowires therefore do not exhibit ideal behavior. Using theoretical and computational models, we predict that optimizing the geometry of split gates in semiconducting heterostructures will lead to higher-quality channels for transport measurements. Further, we show that this optimization is essential for resolving features of interest such as the Rashba-induced spin gap. This new approach to lithographically defined conduction channels provides better energy resolution and is less susceptible to disorder.

title: Pelletization Pressure Engineering of the Superconducting Properties of Fluorine-Doped PrFeAsO
summary: We investigate the influence of the pelletization pressure on the structural, microstructural, and superconducting properties of fluorine-doped PrFeAsO0.7F0.3 (Pr1111). Precursor powders are pressed into pellets at pressures ranging from 174 to 1131 MPa, after which the applied pressure is released and all samples undergo an identical two-step conventional synthesis process at ambient pressure (CSP-AP). All samples predominantly exhibit the tetragonal P4/nmm structure, and the lattice parameter a and unit-cell volume V decrease with increasing pelletization pressure up to an intermediate-pressure range (~900 MPa) before increasing at higher pressures. The actual fluorine-content derived from energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) also increase with pelletization pressure, while Raman spectra show only modest variations in the characteristic vibrational modes associated with Fe and As. The superconducting response exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on the pelletization pressure. Among the investigated samples, the sample pelletized at 870 MPa exhibits the most favorable overall superconducting properties, with a superconducting onset temperature of 44.2 K, ~5 K higher than that of the lowest-pressure sample. It also displays a narrower superconducting transition, the highest relative sample density, a favorable effective magnetic critical current density at high fields, and a relatively large effective thermally activated flux-flow activation energy. At higher pelletization pressures, the superconducting response deteriorates, coinciding with increases in the lattice parameters, increased secondary-phase contributions, and reduced relative density. These findings establish the pelletization pressure as a relevant processing parameter for modifying the structural, microstructural and superconducting properties of Pr1111 during CSP-AP.

title: On transportation of constrictions on phase-lock areas of overdamped Josephson junction by means of isomonodromic deformation of the associated special double confluent Heun equation
summary: An example of computation of locations of constrictions on the phase-lock area in the parameter space for the equation modeling dynamics of overdamped Josephson junction is discussed. Several conjectures of qualitative character are inferred from the heuristic data thus obtained. The method applying isomonodromic deformations of the special double confluent Heun equation associated with the noted model is used. Such a deformation is controlled by the data provided by solution to a Third Painlevè equation for which a new representation in conjunction with the corresponding non-linear second order differential equation fairly efficient in the treatment of the problem in question is proposed.

title: Controlled Oxidation of Tellurium Nanoparticles for Telecom Detection
comment: The main manuscript and Supporting Information have been combined into a single PDF file
summary: Surface oxidation plays an important role in governing charge transport in semiconductor nanoparticle assemblies. Here, we investigate the optoelectronic properties of solution-processed tellurium (Te) nanoparticle ensembles prepared through gradual ambient-air exposure. Structural and spectroscopic analyses reveal interconnected elemental Te nanoparticles with coexisting alpha-TeO2 and hydroxyl-containing surface species, exhibiting a lower relative contribution of oxidized Te than previously investigated forced-air-oxidized ensembles. The resulting photodetectors demonstrate photoresponse at 405, 532, and 1550 nm, with maximum responsivities of 10.1, 14.4, and 8.5 mA/W, respectively. At 1550 nm, the device exhibits rise and fall times of 17.7 and 40.2 s, respectively, and an estimated shot-noise-limited specific detectivity of 1.3 * 10^6 Jones. These findings highlight the importance of controlling surface oxidation to balance interparticle charge transport and dark-current suppression, offering insights for the development of solution-processed Te-based photodetectors for short-wave infrared applications.

title: Energy-resolved current response and the crossover between two approximately linear-in-$T$ resistivity regimes in the infinite-$U$ Hubbard model
summary: We study charge transport in the two-dimensional infinite-$U$ Hubbard model with hopping amplitude $t$ using full exact diagonalization (ED) on $N=16$- and $18$-site square clusters with a single doped hole. We first provide a proof, treating degeneracies explicitly, that a constant dc $f_x$ function, defined as the sum of the squared current matrix elements connecting eigenstates at a given energy to eigenstates of nearly the same energy, averaged over degenerate initial states, is necessary and sufficient for strictly linear-in-$T$ resistivity: $ρ_x(T)=αT$ for all $T>0$ with a constant $α$. The numerically extrapolated dc $f_x$ is not exactly constant, but it is approximately flat over a broad region in the interior of the many-body spectrum and varies strongly within a scale $\varepsilon_{f_x}$ of the spectral edges. This scale $\varepsilon_{f_x}$ is related to a characteristic temperature $T_{\mathrm{cr}}$, which quantifies the leading departure of the resistivity from high-temperature linearity upon cooling. Within the studied temperature range $T/t \geq 0.05$, our ED resistivity results reveal a gradual crossover between high- and low-temperature approximately linear-in-$T$ regimes, with characteristic crossover temperatures $T_{\mathrm{cr}}/t\approx0.414$ and $0.467$ for $N=16$ and $18$, respectively. We also find a broad specific-heat peak associated with this gradual crossover, at $T/t \approx 0.70$ and $0.68$ for $N=16$ and $18$, respectively.

title: Optimised Distillation for Nucleon Correlation Functions
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, Contribution to the 43rd International Symposium on Lattice Field Theory (Lattice 2026)
summary: The calculation and analysis of nucleon correlation functions is essential for understanding the observed spectra and structure of these ubiquitous hadrons. Two challenges arise in their analysis: at early Euclidean times, they are dominated by excited state contributions and at later Euclidean times, the signal-to-noise ratio degrades exponentially. This leads to a common challenge in identifying a reasonable window on which to extract the ground state energy. By modulating the contribution of each Laplacian eigenmode to the correlator via distillation profiles, we build optimised operators which improve the overlap with the nucleon ground state. In these proceedings, we present our progress on constructing optimised distillation profiles for nucleons and their excited state suppression in two- and three-point correlation functions.

title: Ising model on Calandre lattice
summary: In this paper, we proposed to consideration a noval (not yet exploited) planar lattice --- Calandre lattice with the Ising model applied to it. In the framework of an exact analytical Kramers--Wannier transfer-matrix approach and using an extension of the combinatorial Vdovichenko--Feynman method, we have obtained exact solution for Helmholtz free energy and consequent expression for the principal eigenvalue of the Kramers--Wannier transfer-matrix. In addition, we derived the exact expression for spontaneous magnetization. The usage of both expressions made it possible to perform the comprehensive studies of thermodynamic and magnetic properties of the Calandre lattice itself and a wide variety of its affiliated lattices. Among them, diversified interrelations between Calandre lattice and already known and even some novel lattices. These lattices have also revealed such effects as magnetic frustrations, multiple phase transitions and magnetic reentrancy.

title: Coherent Electrometer Using Hybridised Double Quantum Dot - Resonator States
summary: Probing the change in conductance or reactance of a charge sensitive system using an rf cavity is a standard way of doing fast single-charge electrometry. In this article, we present a detector concept which is instead based on coherent interaction. We show that the coherent interaction between a microwave resonator and double quantum dot gives rise to a fast, highly sensitive electrometer. The coherent electrometer achieves a state-of-the-art readout speed, resolving two charge states with SNR of 11.7 in 16 $μ$s, with a readout signal two orders of magnitude lower in power than previously required to reach this speed. In this way, heating of the sample becomes negligible. Thanks to its sensitivity and low dissipation, the coherent electrometer opens up the avenue for quantum limited charge detection with nanosecond speed and minimal back-action.

title: Mimicry of $\textit{d}$-wave Andreev Signatures by Interlayer Pairing
summary: The recent discovery of high-$T_{\rm c}$ superconductivity in bilayer nickelates has attracted enormous attention. Despite dominant theoretical studies pointing to interlayer pairing, the pairing symmetry is strongly debated due to conflicting evidence on nodeless bulk gaps and $d$-wave-like transport signatures. Here, we demonstrate that a nodeless interlayer pairing can naturally mimic $d$-wave Andreev signatures when the point contact is not evenly coupled to the two layers. The phenomenon can be understood by recognizing how a contact potential, which is odd under the layer-exchanging mirror symmetry, acts like an effective Zeeman field on the layer pseudospin. This pseudo field then binds in-gap Andreev states that sweep through the gap with the width and strength of the barrier. We further demonstrate in a realistic model for La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ that the simulated subgap conductance for a top-layer barrier can reproduce the orientation dependent ZBCP usually interpreted as a fingerprint of $\textit{d}$-wave pairing. By revealing this mirror-selective Andreev response from an interlayer pairing state, our work offers a natural scenario to reconcile the conflicting experimental evidence in bilayer nickelates and advances our understanding of unconventional superconductivity.

title: Positivity Improving Quantum Markov Operators
summary: A Markov operator on a matrix algebra, that is, a unital completely positive map, is called positivity improving if it maps every nonzero positive element to an invertible one. This is the noncommutative counterpart of a stochastic matrix with strictly positive entries. We show that positivity improvement is self-dual and equivalent to a faithful quantum Markov--Dobrushin--Doeblin minorization. We also compare the scalar trace minorization with the optimal common-lower-bound construction of the quantum Markov--Dobrushin coefficient. We then characterize positivity improvement through the Kraus space of the map: a Markov operator is positivity improving if and only if the Hilbert--Schmidt orthogonal complement of its Kraus space contains no operator of rank one. As a consequence the Kraus rank of a positivity improving Markov operator on the algebra of $d\times d$ matrices is at least $2d-1$, and an explicit Hankel-type channel shows that this bound is attained in every dimension. Although deciding positivity improvement is NP-hard in general, we obtain complete and effectively checkable classifications for qubits and qutrits, together with families of examples (Pauli, Weyl and Werner--Holevo channels) showing that all our estimates are optimal. Finally we show that, in infinite dimensions, positivity improvement no longer implies any contraction of the Markov operator.

title: Hidden memory above the Neel temperature programs antiferromagnetic order in Cr2O3
summary: Control of antiferromagnetic order is central to magnetoelectric and antiferromagnetic spintronic devices. In the prototypical magnetoelectric antiferromagnet Cr2O3, domains are conventionally selected by simultaneous application of electric and magnetic fields during cooling through the Neel temperature (T_N) or at a fixed temperature below T_N. Here, we show that antiferromagnetic order can instead be programmed by electric-field conditioning entirely in the paramagnetic state above T_N. By measuring the magnetoelectric coefficient (alpha_zz) of bulk Cr2O3 crystals under different thermal and field histories, we find that a sufficiently large electric field above T_N establishes a reversible state that persists after the field is removed. Subsequent magnetic-field cooling with no applied electric field produces a single-domain state with the opposite Neel-vector orientation from conventional magnetoelectric field cooling. The electrically induced state can be reversibly written, erased, and allowed to relax at high temperatures, demonstrating a long-lived internal electric bias that governs domain selection. The observed behavior is consistent with a metastable surface-associated polar state that may generate this internal bias. These results reveal an unexpected coupling between electrically programmed memory and antiferromagnetic domain formation in Cr2O3.

title: On the nature of low-energy electronic states in twisted bilayer graphene: a first-principles study
summary: The nature of low-energy electronic states in twisted bilayer graphene (TBG) near the magic angle has been extensively discussed in the literature on qualitative grounds, since these states play a key role in the construction of effective few-band models toward a many-body theory. Here, we report extensive and systematic first-principles calculations of TBG electronic states in the magic-angle range, using density functional theory with no further approximations. We construct moiré-scale localized Wannier states for the low-energy bands and develop an effective ten-band model for each $K$ valley. The Wannier orbitals contain both atomic and moiré-scale details and are centered near the high-symmetry stackings in the moiré cell. We calculate Coulomb and exchange integrals of these localized states, quantities that are the basic ingredients in many-body models. We also compare the values of these integrals to those obtained or assumed in previous works. By symmetrizing the ten-band Hamiltonians and basis orbitals, we provide insight into how the dominant hoppings between the flat-band orbitals evolve as a function of twist angle.

title: Entanglement percolation enhanced by the power of choice
summary: Quantum communication networks are best supported by maximally entangled states, but imperfections in entanglement generation and distribution generally limit the distributed states to being only partially entangled. Therefore, protocols typically consisting of local operations and classical communication are required to create suitably entangled networks. Here, we introduce a power-of-choice (PoC) protocol based on reversing the selection criteria in the Achlioptas process previously considered in classical explosive percolation. The resulting PoC protocol anticipates the entanglement percolation transition, thereby reducing the entanglement resources needed to establish quantum communication. Notably, in contrast to explosive percolation, the PoC protocol admits an implementation using local information with no appreciable loss of performance.

title: Symanzik Effective Hamiltonian for Lattice Quantum Field Theories
summary: We propose a framework to construct the Symanzik effective Hamiltonian for lattice quantum field theories directly based on dimensional analysis and symmetries in the Hamiltonian formulation. This allows to classify all operators which can contribute at a given order in the spatial lattice spacing. This list can be reduced using the equations of motion and other identities. We exemplify the framework for $φ^4$ and pure gauge theory, obtaining results consistent with earlier publications for the case of classical improvement. It provides the means to develop a non-perturbative improvement programme in the Hamiltonian formulation of lattice quantum field theories in the future.

title: Ergotropy as distance from equilibrium
summary: We show that the ergotropy (a.k.a available energy) of a thermally isolated system is the $1$-Wasserstein distance between two energy probability density functions. Specifically, between the energy profile of the system state, and the energy profile of its associated passive state. We prove this for both classical and quantum systems, and illustrate it with examples. Our result formalises the intuition that ergotropy is a quantifier of distance from equilibrium

title: Extended No-Go Theorem and Its Verification in Spin-Selective Transport through Chiral Cyclodextrin Assemblies
summary: The classical two-terminal single-channel no-go theorem relies on time-reversal symmetry (TRS) and scattering-matrix unitarity. In open systems, omitted channels or environment leakage break unitarity, so TRS and the symplectic reciprocity symmetry TRS\(^{\dagger}\) are no longer equivalent, invalidating the classical premises. We prove that if the two-terminal single-channel scattering matrix satisfies TRS\(^{\dagger}\) plus central inversion symmetry, transmission remains no spin selectivity; this result provides an important complement to the classical no-go theorem in nonunitary regime. When these conditions are violated or the single-channel constraint is lifted, spin-selective transport occurs. In charge transport through devices based on chiral \(γ\)-cyclodextrin molecular assemblies, we verify separately the classical no-go theorem in unitary case and its supplementary version together with its multichannel corollary in nonunitary case: when the conditions for the corresponding no-go theorem hold, the chirality-induced spin selectivity (CISS) of the assembly disappears, whereas when they are violated, CISS emerges. These results extend the no-go theorem to nonunitary scattering systems and establish an effective theoretical framework for studying CISS in real molecular assemblies.

title: Current-voltage characteristics of layered cuprate superconductors with intrinsic Josephson junctions
summary: A brief review of the results for the current-voltage characteristics study in highly anisotropic cuprate superconductors is presented, considering the existence of the intrinsic Josephson effect in multilayer HTSC compounds. We analyzed the observations of multi-branch current-voltage characteristics for current in the c-direction both for the hole-doped and electron-doped cuprate SCs wich conveniently viewed as a strack of intrinsic Josephson junctions, where the CuO2 layers serve as superconducting plates and the buffer layers as dielectric interlayers. It was shown that the tunneling characteristics of intrinsic Josephson junctions in optimally doped p- and n-type cuprates indicate a predominantly d-wave symmetry of the order parameter, demonstrating high conductivity in the subgap regime: U < 2delta/e. The analysis carried out confirms the theoretically predicted power-law dependences U ~ I^gamma with gamma = (0.33 - 0.50) in the hole-doped Bi- and Tl-compounds, which is typical for SCs with monotonic dx^2-y^2 - wave symmetry of the order parameter and with gamma = (0.70 - 0.76) for electron-doped SCs with a non-monotonic d-wave symmetry within the framework of the two-band/two-gap model.

title: Geometric classification of Noether invariants of the Time-Dependent damped Duffing Oscillator
summary: We present a systematic geometric classification of the Noether point symmetries of time-dependent conformal Lagrangians of the form $L = A(t)\left(\frac{1}{2}g_{ij}\dot{x}^{i}\dot{x}^{j} - V(x)\right)$, whose Euler--Lagrange equations describe dynamical systems with time-dependent linear damping. The classification is carried out by coupling the temporal parameters of the conformal factor $A(t)$ with the homothetic algebra of the kinetic metric $g_{ij}$ through a set of compatibility and integrability conditions. The central result is a main theorem which determines the Noether generators, the associated gauge functions and the resulting invariants. The theorem splits naturally into two cases according to whether the quantity $D - 2ψ$ is non-zero or zero, with further subcases depending on whether the homothetic vectors are gradient or non-gradient. The theorem imposes no restrictions on $A(t)$, $g_{ij}$ or $V(x)$, and is therefore fully general and covariant. We apply the theorem to the time-dependent damped Duffing oscillator (DDO) in Euclidean space $E^{3}$ with $A(t) = e^{γt}$ and potential $V = \frac{1}{2}a\,r^{2} + \frac{% λ}{4}r^{4}$. For the damped harmonic oscillator ($λ= 0$) the theorem reproduces the classical Bateman invariant as a special case. For the anharmonic case we obtain a new exact time-dependent quadratic invariant, valid when the linear stiffness satisfies $a = 2γ^{2}/9$. Each invariant is verified explicitly by direct differentiation along the equations of motion. The new invariant provides a rare example of a global conservation law for a fully nonlinear dissipative system, and can be used for the integration and quantization of the DDO.

title: Temperature-Driven Evolution of Magnetization Dynamics in Cobalt-Doped Fe$_5$GeTe$_2$
comment: 26 pages, 5 figures in the main text, 5 figures in Supplementary Information
summary: Understanding magnetization dynamics in metallic van der Waals ferromagnets is essential to uncover their magnetic interactions and evaluate their potential for high-frequency spintronics applications. In this study, we investigate the temperature-dependent magnetization dynamics of a single crystal of cobalt-doped $Fe_{5}GeTe_{2}$ (CFGT) using broadband ferromagnetic resonance (FMR) spectroscopy. At high temperatures, the FMR response is dominated by a single broad resonance that shifts toward lower magnetic fields upon cooling. Fits to the frequency dependence of the resonance field and linewidth yield an effective $g$ factor of approximately 2.45 and an effective Gilbert damping parameter of approximately 0.15 near room temperature. The effective magnetic anisotropy evolves strongly with temperature, with an increasingly pronounced easy-plane contribution upon cooling toward 200 K. Below approximately 200 K, an additional resonance emerges and evolves into a distinct two-mode response that persists to the lowest measured temperature of 25 K. The two branches exhibit different temperature dependences of their resonance fields and linewidths, and the emergence of the additional mode is not accompanied by a comparably pronounced anomaly in the static magnetization. These results reveal a dynamical crossover in CFGT that is not readily apparent from bulk magnetometry and highlight the sensitivity of FMR to the magnetic behavior of chemically substituted van der Waals ferromagnets.

title: Discovery of Kondo-Kramers Nodal Line Topological State in strongly correlated material CeAuAl$_3$
summary: Kramers nodal lines (KNLs) are predicted in all achiral, non-centrosymmetric crystal structures, and yet there are very few experimental realizations of KNLs, only in weakly correlated systems. Especially, their realization in strongly correlated systems remains unexplored. Here we investigate KNL topology in the non-centrosymmetric, achiral Kondo lattice CeAuAl$_3$, using magnetotransport, thermodynamic measurements, density functional theory (DFT), and tight-binding toy model calculations. We find that CeAuAl$_3$ hosts KNLs in the $\mathitΓ\text{-}Z$ and $X\text{-}P$ directions, protected by time-reversal and mirror symmetries. Breaking of these crystalline symmetries, along with time-reversal symmetry via spin polarization, lifts the KNL degeneracy, which, in turn, generates Berry curvature resulting in an intrinsic anomalous Hall effect (AHE). More importantly, CeAuAl$_3$ shows large AHE not only below the magnetic ordering temperature $T_N$ but rather below the Kondo temperature. This underscores the role of the Kondo correlations in bringing the KNLs at the Fermi surface rather than at accidental energies, as would be expected without correlations. Our work identifies a new topological state, Kondo-Kramers Nodal Line, with CeAuAl$_3$ being the first compound explicitly identified to host this new correlated topological state, and demonstrating the expected AHE associated with it. More generally, our work outlines the pathway for finding Kondo-KNL systems in all compounds that combine achiral, non-centrosymmetric structure with Kondo correlations.

title: Bayes-Optimal Quantum Computational Sensing via Convex Spectral Design
summary: Quantum computational sensing performs task-specific inference directly through coherent sensing dynamics, avoiding an intermediate estimation step. Existing designs, however, typically optimize quantum control parameters through nonconvex programs whose performance can depend strongly on initialization. This contribution formulates binary phase classification directly in terms of the sensor's measurement response. For a fixed query budget, generalized quantum signal processing (GQSP) restricts this response to a bounded trigonometric polynomial, while the Bayes classification error is linear in the response. These properties yield an exact finite-dimensional semidefinite program for the globally Bayes-optimal sensor response. Fejér--Riesz factorization and GQSP synthesis then recover a physically realizable control sequence. The same formulation extends naturally to sample-based design and additive phase uncertainty. Numerical tests show improved accuracy and optimization reliability over direct control-angle training; noise-aware redesign also lowers error under phase uncertainty.

title: Unpolarized proton PDF with physical quark masses and large momenta
summary: We present a lattice quantum chromodynamics (QCD) calculation of the proton isovector ($u-d$) unpolarized parton distribution function (PDF) at physical sea and valence quark masses, using Coulomb-gauge-fixed quark bilinears within the large-momentum effective theory framework. The calculation is performed on a (2+1)-flavor ensemble with a lattice spacing of $a=0.076$ fm and proton momenta up to $2.3$ GeV. We combine kinematically enhanced nucleon interpolating operators, the Coulomb-gauge method, and high-statistics measurements to improve the signal quality at large momenta and quark separations. We use the static regularization-independent momentum subtraction and hybrid schemes to renormalize the bare matrix elements. The light-cone PDF in the $\overline{\rm MS}$ scheme is obtained from the quasi-PDF through next-to-leading-order (NLO) perturbative matching supplemented by next-to-leading-logarithmic renormalization-group resummation. With reduced uncertainties, the resulting PDF is consistent with our previous calculation on a similar lattice ensemble with $a=0.06$~fm and a valence pion mass of 300 MeV. Notably, despite the reduced uncertainties, the agreement with the phenomenological PDF persists over the longitudinal momentum fraction range $0.25\lesssim|x|\lesssim0.75$, where the lattice calculation is expected to be reliable. This agreement is further supported by a comparison in coordinate space, where our short-distance lattice matrix elements are consistent with those obtained from the phenomenological PDF through NLO matching. In particular, we observe close agreement in the imaginary part for the first time. Together, these results represent an encouraging step toward precision benchmarking of lattice QCD calculations of PDFs.

title: Computing Classical Partition Functions via Cycle-Space Sampling
summary: We present a method for computing thermodynamic properties of classical spin systems by reformulating the partition function as a sum over even subgraphs of the interaction graph. Starting from the high-temperature expansion, we show that the expansion coefficients are determined by the weight distribution of the null space of the binary incidence matrix over $\mathbb{F}_2$, and that this statement holds verbatim for multi-spin interactions once the graph is replaced by a hypergraph. We introduce a Monte Carlo scheme based on the $1/t$ Wang-Landau algorithm that performs a random walk directly in this null space. Because the weight distribution is temperature independent, a single estimate yields the zero-field partition function, and the thermodynamic quantities obtained from its temperature derivatives, at arbitrary temperature. We validate the approach against exact finite-size results on the two-dimensional triangular-lattice Ising model, apply it to the three- and four-dimensional hypercubic Ising models where no exact solution is available, and to the two- and three-dimensional Baxter-Wu models, whose three-spin interactions place them outside the reach of Pfaffian methods. For the two-body models we compare against conventional Wang-Landau sampling in energy space; for the Baxter-Wu models we validate against exact enumeration at the smallest size in each dimension.

title: Probing Chern Topology through Hall-Sensitive Photonic Spin Hall Shifts in a d-wave Altermagnet
summary: In this paper, we investigate the photonic spin Hall effect in a two-dimensional Rashba-coupled $d$-wave altermagnetic Chern system subjected to a uniform out-of-plane exchange field. We first analyze the energy-band structure and the Dirac mass distribution at the high-symmetry points, where $m_Γ=m_M=Δ_x, m_X=Δ_x-4 t_J$, and $m_Y=Δ_x+4 t_J$. Band inversions at high-symmetry points generate both a topologically trivial regime $(C=0)$ and Chern-insulating phases $(C= \pm 1)$. Employing the Kubo formalism for the optical conductivity together with the reflection matrix for a substrate-supported conducting sheet, we compute helicity-dependent finite-waist displacements of a reflected Gaussian beam. The resulting optical response exhibits a minimum interband absorption threshold, a Van Hove-type spectral feature, and distinct transitions at the $X$ and $Y$ points arising from the momentum dependence of the exchange field. Under the specified Hall-tensor and polarization sign conventions, the longitudinal helicity half-separation is odd upon reversal of the optical Hall conductivity and correspondingly changes sign between opposite-Chern phases, whereas the transverse half-separation is even in the Hall response. The maximal spin-dependent splitting occur in the vicinity of the pseudo-Brewster reflectance minimum. The longitudinal spin splitting reverses sign between opposite Chern phases, reflecting the exchange-controlled optical Hall response, while its pronounced spectral variations reveal the influence of inequivalent interband transitions induced by the $d$-wave altermagnetic exchange. These findings establish polarization-resolved photonic beam shifts as a sensitive probe of Hall-active topological phases and their characteristic optical spectra.

title: Transverse quasiparticle heat transport in p-wave magnetic Josephson junctions
summary: We study transverse heat currents carried by Bogoliubov quasiparticles in $p$-wave magnetic Josephson junctions under a longitudinal temperature bias. We find that such a junction supports a transverse spin heat current while the net transverse heat current vanishes. This effect stems from the $p$-wave magnetism, which shifts the two spin sectors oppositely in transverse momentum space and thereby causes them to carry opposite heat currents. A weak Zeeman field lifts the compensation between the two spin-sector contributions, thereby generating a finite net transverse heat current. The directions of both currents can be switched by reversing the sign of the $p$-wave magnetic splitting or tuning the superconducting phase difference, while both currents vanish in the absence of $p$-wave magnetism. These findings highlight $p$-wave magnetic Josephson junctions as a versatile platform for switchable transverse heat transport and controllable spin caloritronics.

title: The random matrix hard edge --- applications, exact PDFs and large $N$ expansions
summary: A hard edge of a Hermitian random matrix occurs when the eigenvalue density is strictly zero on one side of the edge, and nonzero on the other. Another possibility is that the eigenvalues occur in $\pm$ pairs, which creates a hard edge at the origin for the positive eigenvalues. Both review material and new results are presented for random matrix ensembles exhibiting a hard edge. The review material has two focuses: one is on applications of the random matrix hard edge, while the other is on exact eigenvalue probability density functions. The new results relate to the large $N$ expansion of correlation functions and conditioned gap probability generating functions with hard edge scaling for the Jacobi ensemble. For all even $β$ we are able to show that these quantities admit expansions in inverse even powers of the variable $N_{\rm hJ}':= N - 1/2 + (a + b + 1)/β$. For the $β=2$ Jacobi unitary ensemble, we can relate the leading (next leading) correction to the limit law to a particular second order (fourth order) differential operator applied to the latter. The analogous second order differential operator is found for $β=1,4$, leading then to its conjectured form for all $β>0$.

title: A Transport-Constrained Gradient-Flow Description of Continuum Dislocation Dynamics
comment: Accepted to appear in Journal of the Mechanics and Physics of Solids
summary:
Gradient flow frameworks are fundamental to numerous models of defect and microstructure evolution. This work develops a gradient flow formulation for continuum dislocation dynamics, with the key distinction that the admissible rates are transport-constrained. Using the dislocation density and compatible slip fields as the primary state variables, their admissible rates are restricted by geometric conservation laws. The corresponding transport velocities are then selected variationally through a constrained Onsager principle. The resulting model has both a variational gradient flow structure and consistency with the geometric dislocation conservation statement; existing models of dislocation evolution typically have either one or the other feature.
  This thermodynamic structure provides a dislocation driving force that includes elastic stress contributions -- corresponding to the classical Peach--Koehler force -- as well as contributions from the core and nonconvex lattice energies. A simplified version of the model is used to study the energetics and dynamics of an opposite-sign dislocation pair. The lattice energy keeps the cores compact, and an external applied shear either assists annihilation or, above a threshold, separates the pair.

title: Momentum-Resolved Kondo Hybridization of Nonsymmorphic Dirac-Derived Bands in CeAgBi$_2$
summary: How symmetry-constrained conduction states acquire heavy-quasiparticle character is a central question in correlated quantum materials. Combining angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, Ce $4d \rightarrow 4f$ resonant photoemission, and first-principles calculations, we investigate the nonsymmorphic Kondo lattice CeAgBi$_2$. We identify quasi-two-dimensional Bi-square-net-derived bands consistent with calculated Dirac crossings and nodal lines. Resonant photoemission resolves a nearly dispersionless Ce 4$f$ band near the Fermi level, establishing Kondo heavy-quasiparticle states. Its pronounced momentum-dependent spectral weight at intersections with the identified Dirac-derived branches provides direct spectroscopic evidence for their participation in $c$-$f$ hybridization. Complementary measurements on independently cleaved samples and an effective hybridization model connect these branches to the Kondo heavy-quasiparticle spectrum. The combined results support preservation of nonsymmorphic Dirac-band connectivity under Kondo renormalization, showing how symmetry-constrained conduction states become constituents of correlated heavy quasiparticles.

title: Symplectic Reck: In-Situ Learning of Gaussian Quantum Operations
summary: Programmable photonic circuits are a natural platform for physical learning, where hardware parameters are trained directly from measured feedback. We propose a physical learning algorithm and architecture for continuous-variable quantum systems where a photonic circuit is trained in situ to invert an unknown lossless Gaussian quantum operation. We prove that a generic symplectic matrix $S\in\mathrm{Sp}(2N,\mathbb{R})$ admits a decomposition into a triangular array of two-mode symplectic gates on neighboring modes, followed by single-mode symplectic gates. We then introduce the symplectic Reck mesh, which physically realizes this factorization, generalizing the unitary Reck mesh widely used in optical neural networks. When placed after an unknown Gaussian unitary, the mesh is trained in situ by nulling local response blocks one at a time using optical probes and measurements. We identify a local condition number that quantifies the squeezing required for a nulling step and its sensitivity to measurement error. We numerically demonstrate finite-shot training and robustness to systematic gate-calibration errors. Our work extends self-configuring optical networks from unitary to symplectic transformations, bringing physical learning to continuous-variable quantum photonic hardware.

title: The structure of the pion at large $N_c$
summary: We compute the pion quark momentum fraction in the large-$N_c$ limit using the Twisted Eguchi-Kawai (TEK) reduced model. Gauge configurations for different values of the lattice spacing are generated with the pure-gauge TEK action, while the pion correlators are computed for different quark masses with maximally twisted mass fermions. The bare matrix element corresponding to the quark momentum fraction is obtained using the Feynman-Hellmann method, and we use perturbative renormalization factors to connect to the $\overline{\mathrm{MS}}$ scheme at $2\,\mathrm{GeV}$. A global analysis at several lattice spacings, pion masses, and values of $N_c$ yields $\langle x\rangle_q^{\overline{\mathrm{MS}}}(2\,\mathrm{GeV}) = 0.267(105)$ at the physical pion mass in the large-$N_c$ limit. This value is significantly smaller than existing $N_c=3$ determinations from phenomenology and lattice QCD, indicating that, in the large-$N_c$ limit, the pion's light-cone momentum is carried predominantly by gluons.

title: The role of preparation protocols in the Mpemba effect under time-delayed Newton cooling
summary: The Mpemba effect depends on both the relaxation dynamics and the protocol used to prepare the initial states. Here, this dependence is investigated using the time-delayed Newton cooling law, comparing protocols in which two samples are exposed to piecewise-constant bath temperatures before being placed in a common final bath. For protocols with at most two quenches and a common waiting time, exact conditions for the occurrence of the effect are derived. They rule out the Pontus protocol within this model and show that the synchronous two-reservoir protocol maximizes the effect magnitude within the class considered. The robustness of this optimum is then examined by allowing asynchronous quenches or an additional quench for one sample. Numerical optimization of these extensions identifies the synchronous two-reservoir protocol as the maximizing limit in the cases studied. This evidence motivates a conjecture that the same protocol remains optimal for more general bath histories, although that broader statement is not proved.

title: 2D coherent spectroscopy of topological insulators
summary: Multidimensional coherent spectroscopy probes the response of a system to a sequence of time-separated light pulses, and has attracted significant interest in recent years. In the frequency space, it generates multidimensional spectra, in which information about different degrees of freedom of the system is generically disentangled. In this work, we develop a quantum geometric formulation of multidimensional optical susceptibilities in insulating systems. Focusing on a two-pulse setup and working in the velocity gauge, we derive analytical expressions for second-order and third-order two-dimensional coherent spectra (2DCS). We focus on the third-order ABB response, which remains finite in centrosymmetric systems where the second-order susceptibility vanishes by inversion symmetry. Its paramagnetic contribution supports an echo signal that probes products of four interband Berry-connection matrix elements, which reduce in two-band systems to bilinear combinations of the quantum geometric tensor of the occupied band. Using continuum and square-lattice models of two-dimensional Chern insulators, we show how the echo resolves the momentum-space sign structure of these geometric quantities. For the $xxyx$ response of the models considered, the number of nodes in the echo signal is related to the band topology. Our results extend the quantum-geometric interpretation of multidimensional spectroscopy to higher-order responses, showing that third-order 2DCS provides access to geometric structures beyond those probed at lower orders.

title: Pseudogap in hole doped cuprates: a status report
summary: The pseudogap state, an anomalous momentum dependent partial suppression of low energy electronic excitations persisting well above the superconducting critical temperature in underdoped cuprates, remains one of the most profound enigmas in condensed physics today. This review summarizes over three decades of experimental and theoretical progress. It appears that pseudogap is not a mere precursor to superconductivity, but a distinct, intertwined state of matter characterized by a complex interplay of competing and cooperating electronic orders. We critically examine the bulk probes like resistivity and magnetic susceptibility and the surface hallmark spectroscopic signatures observed via angle resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) in this review. ARPES reveals a Fermi surface truncated into disconnected segments and scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) visualizes a spatially heterogeneous energy gap around the Fermi level. These observations are contextualized alongside transport anomalies, including resistivity and bulk magnetic susceptibility, to construct a phenomenological portrait of a phase that violates conventional Fermi liquid theory. By mapping the electronic phase diagram, we highlight the abrupt transition at above optimal doping. We conclude with open questions still to be answered. This review underscores the role of the pseudogap as a key to unlocking the unconventional pairing mechanism of hole doped cuprates and the broader physics of strongly correlated electron systems.

title: Cylinder spectral curve and 1-cut Matrix model
summary: For a random matrix, with eigenvalues in a one-body potential $V(x)$ and a 2-body interaction $R(x,x')$, it is known that the resolvent converges in the large $N$ limit to an analytic function in the complex plane minus cuts, called the spectral curve. In the 1-cut case, a two-sheeted neighborhood of the cut is a cylinder with two simple ramification points. We describe these spectral curve data by boundary integral operators and generalized cycles. Vice-versa, given a 2-branchpoints spectral curve in a cylinder, there exists a formal random matrix model that corresponds to it. The goal of this article is to show the method to recover a formal random matrix model, with its potential and 2-body interaction, from the geometry of the spectral curve.

title: Atomically abrupt sp-sp$^2$ all-carbon heterojunction preserving the electronic identity of constituent allotropes
summary: Covalently integrating distinct carbon allotropes with atomic precision remains, to date, elusive, despite the clear advantage of combining complementary functionalities while preserving their electronic identities. Here, we realize an all-carbon lateral heterojunction combining ($sp^2$) armchair graphene nanoribbons (GNRs) and $sp$-$sp^2$ hydrogenated graphdiyne (hGDY) on Au(111) through Fe-mediated hierarchical on-surface synthesis. Low-temperature scanning tunnelling microscopy and spectroscopy combined with density-functional theory reveal an atomically abrupt (<0.5 nm), asymmetric type-I interface. Redistribution of an edge-localized GNR state onto the first hGDY unit demonstrates local electronic continuity, whereas their characteristic electronic structures re-emerge immediately beyond the interface. Calculations further indicate that heterojunction formation weakens the interaction of both constituents with the underlying Au(111) substrate, widening their gaps and reducing adsorption-induced interfacial polarization. These results establish lateral covalent integration as a route to engineer atomically defined electronic interfaces and substrate coupling in all-carbon nanostructures.

title: Quartet ferromagnetism in the small-exchange limit
summary: Rare-earth magnets are often regarded as classical owing to their large angular momentum J, but this picture breaks down when exchange is smaller than the crystalline electric-field (CEF) energy scale, allowing the degeneracy of low-lying CEF manifolds to dictate the emergent quantum phases. Here, we uncover such a regime in the RV6Sn6 (R = rare-earth) kagome metals with strong magnetic anisotropy. Thermodynamic and neutron-diffraction measurements reveal successive axial and tilted ferromagnetic (FM) phases in DyV6Sn6, arising from independent ordering of the axial Mz and transverse Mx dipolar components enabled by a rare quasi-quartet ground state. On the other hand, HoV6Sn6 has a similar tilted magnetic anisotropy, but remains axial down to 0.03 K. This discrepancy can be traced back to the non-Kramers nature of Ho3+ where the CEF lifts the quartet degeneracy, leaving a quasi-triplet ground state. Unlike quartets or higher multiplets, we find that the effective spin-1 triplet does not allow independent dipolar ordering without strong quadrupolar (nematic) interactions that act to break rotational symmetry, revealing an essential multipolar prerequisite for tilted magnetic ground states. These results establish a quartet CEF manifold as the minimal degeneracy required for dipolar-driven independent ordering. Mapping the surrounding CEF parameter space further reveals competing magnetic, non-magnetic singlet, and potential quadrupolar phases, driven by multifold ground state degeneracies. These results establish CEF tuning as a versatile route to unconventional quantum phases across the broader RT6X6 (T = transition metal; X = Sn, Ge) family.

title: Can One Hear the Size of a Clock?
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures; Supplemental Material (12 pages) included
summary: Weyl's law counts the vibration modes that fit into a cavity, and a quantum system with $d$ levels can oscillate at up to $d(d-1)/2$ frequencies without decay. For systems that jump at random between states, no such count was known: they oscillate only out of equilibrium, and the random timing of their jumps damps every oscillation. We find the missing count: if $Q$ is the ratio of frequency to decay rate, a system of $d$ states sustains fewer than $2(d-1)/(πQ)$ oscillations whose ratio exceeds $Q$. Nested cycles approach this bound, and measured oscillations reveal how large a hidden system must be.

title: A regularization-independent Information Criterion for correlated data
summary: We generalize the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) to allow model and data subset selection when regularized fits are performed on correlated data. While the standard generalization to regularized fits is inherently dependent on the type of regularization applied to the data covariance matrix, our definition, the RIAIC, is, on average, regularization-independent. The regularization-independence is achieved by defining the new Information Criterion as an estimator of the model-dependent contribution to the correlated Kullback--Leibler divergence. The Bayesian extension is derived as well. We test the new criterion on lattice QCD data by performing regularized fits and show that it reproduces the selection properties of the standard correlated AIC, with fluctuations which are compatible with the expected statistical uncertainties. These results enable the application of subset and model selection techniques to cases where regularizations are applied to the covariance matrix of the fitted dataset.

title: Discrete time crystals stabilized by bounded measurement noise
summary: Periodically driven clean interacting systems generically heat up, which destroys discrete time-crystalline order. Here we ask whether continuous weak measurement can stabilize such order. We study a long-range interacting spin chain whose local occupation is continuously monitored. Measurements generally induce a transition from volume-law to area-law entanglement. Yet low entanglement alone is not enough: along typical quantum trajectories, the system still reaches a featureless state with no subharmonic response. In contrast, the most-probable trajectory, obtained by suppressing measurement fluctuations, shows robust period doubling. To connect these limits, we introduce a bounded-noise protocol that restricts measurement fluctuations to a finite window. Narrow windows preserve period doubling. Intermediate windows produce coexisting time-crystalline and non-time-crystalline trajectories. Over time, trajectories leave the time-crystalline group one by one, so the order is long lived but finite. Wide windows destroy the order. Our results establish bounded measurement noise, discarding the large-deviation trajectories, as a route to time-crystalline order in clean systems. They also show that the measurement-induced area-law phase is necessary, but not sufficient, for this order.

title: Imaging spin entanglement with a scanning tunneling microscope
summary: Artificial spin arrays assembled on surfaces enable atomic-scale studies of quantum correlations. Here we establish a hierarchy of connections between spin inelastic electron tunneling spectroscopy (IETS) and entanglement in spin-$1/2$ systems. We first show that the number of spectroscopically active transitions in a spin-$1/2$ dimer serves as an entanglement witness. Using the leading-order tunneling conductance for the tip placed on spin $i$, $dI(i)/dV$, we then relate spectral moments $\mathcal{M}^{(n)}(i)=\int V^n(d^2I(i)/dV^2)\,dV$ to quantum correlations. The zeroth moment probes the one-tangle in systems with a gapped, nondegenerate ground state. For rotationally invariant Heisenberg systems, the first moment yields thermal spin correlators $\langle\boldsymbol S(i)\cdot\boldsymbol S(j)\rangle$, enabling reconstruction of nearest-neighbor concurrence and spatial imaging of entanglement in spin chains. It also provides access to the internal energy and magnetic specific heat, both usable as entanglement witnesses. Applying this approach to experimental IETS data from nanographene spin chains, we find good agreement with theory. We further discuss how the second moment probes longer-range correlations and the inverse moment relates to local spin susceptibility. For spin-$1/2$ trimers, we connect inter-multiplet inelastic spectral weight to genuine tripartite entanglement quantified by the concurrence fill. Finally, we reconcile the local character of IETS with its sensitivity to nonlocal entanglement through an analogy with digital quantum circuits, where Hamiltonian evolution implements multiqubit operations. These results establish IETS as a tool for quantifying and imaging entanglement in engineered on-surface spin systems.

title: Ferromagnetic resonance signatures of edge states for distinguishing chiral and helical $p$-wave superconductors
summary: We theoretically investigate ferromagnetic resonance (FMR) modulation at interfaces between ferromagnetic insulators and two-dimensional chiral and helical $p$-wave superconductors. We evaluate the surface dynamical spin susceptibility, including both edge and bulk quasiparticle excitations. For momentum-conserving interfacial exchange at zero temperature, the edge contribution to the Gilbert damping exhibits distinct frequency scalings for the excitation energies well above the spectral broadening, $\hbarω\gg2δ$: $δ/(\hbarω)^{2}$ for the chiral state and $1/\hbarω$ for the helical state. For a clean superconducting boundary, edge-induced Ising spin anisotropy persists even when interfacial exchange disorder randomizes momentum transfer. The low-energy edge response is suppressed when the magnetization aligns with the edge-state spin axis. These results establish FMR modulation as a probe complementary to existing methods for distinguishing the chiral and helical states and constraining their $d$-vector directions.

title: Exactly integrable field theory in $(2+1)$-dimensional space-time: the spectral equations
summary: The primary object in quantum field theories is the one-step relativistic evolution operator. In this paper we consider the evolution operator defined on the auxiliary Kagomé lattice with the $q$-oscillator algebra of observables, the local ingredient of the evolution operator is the $q$-oscillator $R$-matrix of the Zamolodchikov tetrahedron equation. We construct explicitly the complete system of equations (which can be seen as a specific form of nested Bethe Ansatz equations) defining the spectrum of the evolution operator. This system of equations is valid for an arbitrary initial data (occupation numbers), and the thermodynamical limit is well defined for this system.

title: Fabrication and Characterization of Flexible In2O3 Thin-Film Transistors on Mica Substrates
summary: Flexible oxide-semiconductor thin-film transistors (TFTs) with high field-effect mobility (uFE > 70 cm^2/Vs) are required for next-generation flexible displays. Polycrystalline In2O3-based TFTs are promising candidates; however, conventional flexible substrates such as plastics are not suitable because their fabrication typically requires relatively high temperatures (~350 deg.C). In this study, we used mica as a flexible substrate to fabricate polycrystalline In2O3-based TFTs, motivated by previous demonstrations of crystalline oxide growth on mica. The resulting TFTs exhibited a uFE of approximately 75 cm^2/Vs. The devices maintained gate-modulated operation after 10^3 flex-out bending cycles at a 5 mm radius, whereas flex-in cycling caused early electrical failure, likely due to In2O3 film degradation. The TFTs also operated normally after exposure to 85 deg.C and 40% relative humidity for one day. These results demonstrate that mica substrates enable high-mobility, flex-out-compatible In2O3-based TFTs.

title: Dipolar Exchange and Emergent Electric-Dipole-Carrying Quasiparticles in Electronic Ferroelectrics
summary: Electronic correlations underpin diverse spontaneously ordered states in matter, whose collective excitations emerge as quasiparticles that encode the underlying order. While spin exchange interactions give rise to magnetic order and its quasiparticle excitations known as magnons, their counterparts in electronic ferroelectrics remain poorly understood. Here, we derive an analogous quantum dipolar-pseudospin exchange model for electronic ferroelectricity and identify the associated bosonic quasiparticles that carry intrinsic electric dipole moments. Unlike ferrons in conventional lattice-based ferroelectrics, these dipolar quasiparticles arise entirely from collective electronic dynamics without involving lattice vibrations. Their excitation spectrum exhibits a linear Stark shift under a static electric field, while coupling to an oscillating electric field enables their coherent excitation, leading to colossal, resonantly enhanced second-harmonic generation and optical rectification in the terahertz regime. These dipolar quasiparticles offer promising opportunities for electrically tunable nonlinear optics and open a route toward extending the paradigm of transport in electronic systems beyond conventional charge currents to electric dipole currents.

title: Experimental visual quantum state discrimination
summary: Almost all solutions to vision tasks $\unicode{x2014}$ offered by nature and technology alike $\unicode{x2014}$ rely on capturing an image using a lens or a similar optical instrument, followed by computational analysis by neurons of a brain or a digital computer. This approach is inherently suboptimal in photon-limited and noisy conditions, where critical information is irreversibly lost at the measurement stage. We address this gap by introducing AI-driven optimization of quantum measurements on the incoming photons, learning how to extract the maximum possible information for a given computer vision task from each incoming photon. The trained measurement consists of a diffractive optical neural network (DONN) followed by a detector array. We train the DONN with a quantum information-theoretic objective that maximizes the rate at which the discrimination error decays as photons accumulate. The resulting measurement achieves exponentially lower error than both direct imaging and a DONN optimized for single-photon discrimination. We validate the advantage in a noiseless setting as well as a photon-counting experiment with an electron-multiplying CCD with the noise corresponding to $10^4$ photons per single signal photon, where the measurement also learns to mitigate the detector noise.

title: Deriving Tsallis Entropy from First Principles
summary: The kinetic approach for q-distribution is extended through a "bottom-up" procedure to the corresponding entropic formula. In this way, the validity of Tsallis' formula, S_q(W) = k_B ln_q(W), is established from first principles. The resulting q-entropy is additive and the zeroth law of thermodynamics is automatically satisfied because the conventional identification beta = 1/(k_B T) remains valid. Entropy, energy, and all relevant quantities for both discrete and continuous cases are evaluated using standard (linear) averages. The "bottom-up" and "top-down" approaches yield the same q-distribution for velocities. The standard results are naturally recovered in the limit q -> 1.

title: Electron cooling mediated by transverse optical phonons in doped SrTiO$_3$
summary: Soft transverse optical (TO) phonons in doped SrTiO$_3$ couple to electrons through the polarization field, quadratically in the paraelectric phase and, additionally, linearly in the polar phase due to the onset of spontaneous polarization. We investigate heat flow between a three-dimensional electron gas and soft TO phonons. For two-TO-phonon scattering, the heat flow of hot electrons crosses over from $T^5$ to $T^3$ at the Bloch-Gruneisen temperature. In the polar phase, an additional one-TO-phonon channel emerges, yielding a softer temperature dependence of the heat flow, $T^3$ at low and $T$ at high temperatures, with the spectral weight set by the spontaneous polarization. This channel may dominate at low temperatures and leads to a nonmonotonic temperature dependence of the heat flow in the vicinity of the polar transition.

title: Identifying Contributions to the Superconducting Diode Effect through Nonreciprocal Superconducting Properties
summary: Nonreciprocal superconducting responses provide a sensitive probe of superconducting states in systems where inversion and time-reversal symmetries are broken. However, in the superconducting diode effect (SDE), where the critical current differs for opposite current directions, nonreciprocity can also arise from vortex-induced contributions caused by minute magnetic field misalignment, complicating its interpretation. Here, we investigate a noncentrosymmetric $[Nb/V/Ta]_{40}$ superlattice and demonstrate nonreciprocity in all three fundamental superconducting properties: the critical current, critical field, and superconducting transition temperature.
